title: Web Crawler Multithreaded
statement:
On LeetCode this is a multithreading problem: there `getUrls` is a slow blocking call and a crawler that fetches one page at a time runs out of time. Here `getUrls` returns a promise, and you speed the crawl up by running fetches concurrently instead of with threads.

Write `crawl(startUrl, htmlParser)`, an async function that returns every page you can reach from `startUrl` without leaving its hostname. `htmlParser.getUrls(url)` returns a promise of the list of urls that the page `url` links to, and each call takes 15 ms. The rules:

- Begin at `startUrl` and follow links, but only to urls with the same hostname as `startUrl`; never call `getUrls` for a url on another hostname.
- Never fetch the same url twice.
- Every url looks like `http://hostname` or `http://hostname/path` (no port), so its hostname is the text between `http://` and the next `/`. Hostnames must match exactly: `example.org` and `a.example.org` are different.
- Resolve with `startUrl` and every same-hostname url you reached, each once, in any order.

Each case gives `urls`, `edges` and `startUrl`: `edges[j] = [a, b]` means that the page `urls[a]` links to `urls[b]`. The answer is `{ urls, time }`: the urls `crawl` returned, sorted, and the time in ms at which its promise resolved. Let `D` be the largest number of links needed to reach a crawled page from `startUrl` through crawled pages; the crawl must finish at `15 * (D + 1)` ms. That is what you get by fetching every page as soon as it is discovered (or a whole breadth-first level at a time, in parallel); fetching one page at a time is too slow.
constraints: urls are distinct and have the form http://hostname or http://hostname/path, with no port
A hostname is 1 to 63 characters of lowercase letters, digits, dots and hyphens, and does not start or end with a hyphen
edges[j] = [a, b] with 0 <= a, b < urls.length
signature: Object crawl(String[] urls, int[][] edges, String startUrl)
api: crawl(startUrl: string, htmlParser: { getUrls(url: string): Promise<string[]> }): Promise<string[]>
notes:
## Intuition

Crawling is a graph search: pages are nodes, links are edges, and only same-hostname pages may be expanded. The only twist is time. Each fetch takes 15 ms, so fetching pages one after another costs 15 ms per page, while fetching every known page at once costs 15 ms per *level* of the search. So start a fetch for each new page the moment it is discovered, and keep one shared `seen` set so that two fetches never discover and expand the same page. The crawl is done when every fetch, and every fetch those started, has finished. (The brute force runs a breadth-first search one level at a time, fetching each whole level in parallel; with equal fetch times it finishes at the same moment.)

## Approach

1. Extract the hostname as the third piece of `url.split('/')` and remember `host`, the hostname of `startUrl`.
2. Put `startUrl` in `seen` and call `visit(startUrl)`.
3. `visit(url)` awaits `getUrls(url)`. For each link that is new and on `host`, it adds the link to `seen` **before** fetching it and starts `visit(link)` without waiting.
4. `visit` then awaits `Promise.all` of the visits it started, so `visit(startUrl)` finishes only when the whole crawl has.
5. Return the contents of `seen`.

With real threads, `seen` becomes a concurrent set (`ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()` in Java, whose `add` tells you atomically whether the url is new), and each new url is submitted to a thread pool. The crawl ends when a counter of unfinished tasks drops to zero, or when all submitted futures are complete. Marking a url before fetching it is what keeps two threads from crawling it twice.

## Example 1, step by step

`startUrl = "http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/"`, so `host = "news.yahoo.com"`.

- 0 ms: fetch `/news/topics/`. At 15 ms it returns `http://news.yahoo.com` and `/news`, both new and on `host`: both go into `seen` and both fetches start.
- 30 ms: `http://news.yahoo.com` returns `/us`, which is new: fetch it. `/news` links nowhere.
- 45 ms: `/us` returns nothing, every visit is finished, and `crawl` resolves.
- The answer is the four `news.yahoo.com` urls, sorted, with `time: 45` (three levels of 15 ms). `http://news.google.com` is never reached: nothing on the crawled pages links to it.

## Complexity

- Time: O(V + E) work for the V pages and E links examined, and 15 * (D + 1) ms of waiting, where D is the depth of the search.
- Space: O(V) for `seen` and the visits in flight.

## Pitfalls

- Comparing hostnames with `startsWith` or `includes`: `example.org.uk`, `a.example.org` and `http://other.com/example.org` all contain `example.org`.
- Adding a url to `seen` only after its fetch returns: two pages that link to it would then both fetch it.
- Awaiting each `visit` inside the loop makes the crawl sequential again and far too slow.
- A same-hostname page linked only from another hostname's page is not reachable: you may not fetch the foreign page.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `host` | the hostname of `startUrl`; only urls with this hostname are crawled |
| `seen` | every url already discovered (and so fetched or being fetched) |
| `visit` | fetches one page and crawls its new links concurrently |
| `links` | the urls that the page being visited links to |
| `fetches` | the visits started for this page's new links |

narration.3: Only pages on this hostname may be crawled.
narration.4: seen records every url already discovered, starting with startUrl itself.
narration.6: Fetch the page; this is the 15 ms wait.
narration.8: Look at every link on the page.
narration.9: Skip links already discovered and links to other hostnames.
narration.10: Mark the link before fetching it, so no other visit fetches it again.
narration.11: Start crawling the link right away, without waiting for it.
narration.13: This page is done once every visit it started is done.
narration.15: The crawl starts at startUrl and ends when the whole tree of visits has finished.
